---
title: "The chi-squared distribution"

The normal page estimated a mean and variance for each /i/ F1 speaker group. Under an independent normal-sampling model, the uncertainty in an estimated variance has a **chi-squared reference distribution**.

We construct that reference statistic, connect its degrees of freedom to the number of centered vowel measurements, and then use the resulting density to interpret variance uncertainty under the normal model.

## Definition

If $Z_1,\ldots,Z_\nu$ are independent standard-normal variables, then

$$
Q=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}Z_j^2
\sim\chi^2_\nu.
$$

Its density is

$$
f_Q(q)
=\frac{q^{\nu/2-1}e^{-q/2}}
       {2^{\nu/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)},
\qquad q>0,
$$

with

$$
\mathbb{E}[Q]=\nu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Q]=2\nu.
$$

The moments follow from independence and the standard-normal moments:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Q]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}\mathbb{E}[Z_j^2]
=\nu,\\
\operatorname{Var}[Q]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}\operatorname{Var}[Z_j^2]
=2\nu.
\end{aligned}
$$

For an independent sample from $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$,

$$
\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}.
$$

Here is the missing link. Standardize the sample as
$Z_i=(X_i-\mu)/\sigma$. The total standardized sum of squares decomposes into
orthogonal mean and residual components:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{X_i-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2
=\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{X_i-\overline X}{\sigma}\right)^2
+n\left(\frac{\overline X-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2.
$$

The left side is a sum of $n$ independent squared standard normals. Under
normal sampling, the projection onto the sample-mean direction and the
projection onto the residual subspace are independent. The mean component uses
one dimension, leaving an $(n-1)$-dimensional residual component. Since

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{X_i-\overline X}{\sigma}\right)^2
=\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2},
$$

that component has the $\chi^2_{n-1}$ distribution. Estimating the mean thus
removes one freely varying direction; it is not a convention attached after
the fact.

## Degrees of freedom from the vowel data

The degrees of freedom below are not illustrative choices. They come from the numbers of speakers who produced /i/ in the [Hillenbrand dataset](continuous-random-variables.qmd).

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-chi-square
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
i_tokens <- subset(vowels, vowel == "i")
group_sizes <- as.data.frame(table(i_tokens$speaker_type), responseName = "n")
names(group_sizes)[1] <- "speaker_type"
group_sizes$df <- group_sizes$n - 1L
group_sizes$reference_mean <- group_sizes$df
group_sizes$reference_variance <- 2 * group_sizes$df

chi_grid <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(group_sizes)), function(j) {
  df <- group_sizes$df[j]
  q <- seq(0, qchisq(0.999, df), length.out = 400L)
  data.frame(speaker_type = group_sizes$speaker_type[j], df = df,
             q = q, density = dchisq(q, df))
}))

adult_men <- subset(group_sizes, speaker_type == "man")
adult_men_interval <- qchisq(c(0.025, 0.975), df = adult_men$df)

stopifnot(
  sum(group_sizes$n) == 139L,
  all(group_sizes$df == group_sizes$n - 1L),
  all(group_sizes$reference_variance == 2 * group_sizes$reference_mean)
)

group_sizes
adult_men_interval
```

For adult men, $\nu=$ `r adult_men$df`. The reference mean is thus `r adult_men$reference_mean` and the reference variance is `r adult_men$reference_variance`. The central reference interval runs from `r sprintf("%.2f", adult_men_interval[1])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", adult_men_interval[2])`.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-chi-square
#| fig-cap: "Chi-squared reference densities whose degrees of freedom come from the observed /i/ speaker-group sizes."
ggplot(chi_grid, aes(q, density, group = speaker_type,
                     linetype = speaker_type, color = speaker_type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_grey(start = 0.2, end = 0.7) +
  labs(x = expression(chi^2), y = "Reference density",
       color = "Speaker group", linetype = "Speaker group") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

There is deliberately no observed chi-squared statistic in this plot. Computing $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2$ requires a specified population variance $\sigma^2$, and the dataset does not supply one. The curves show how the reference changes with an empirically determined sample size; later inference pages will use that reference to reason about an unknown variance.

Keep three objects separate. $Q=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}Z_j^2$ is the abstract random
construction. $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2$ is the random variance statistic under a
normal-sampling model. A realized value $q$ can be computed only after both the
sample and the candidate $\sigma^2$ are specified.

## Check your understanding

1. Confirm each degree of freedom from the raw /i/ rows.
2. Why does the variance statistic use $n-1$ degrees of freedom?
3. Use `qchisq()` to compute the corresponding central interval for another speaker group.
4. Why would substituting the sample variance for $\sigma^2$ erase the inferential question?
5. Which assumption licenses independence of the mean and residual components
   in the projection argument?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The raw /i/ groups contain 27 boys, 19 girls, 45 men, and 48 women, giving 26, 18, 44, and 47 degrees of freedom, respectively. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The variance statistic has $n-1$ degrees of freedom because estimating the sample mean imposes the constraint that the centered deviations sum to zero. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. For the 48 women, `qchisq(c(.025, .975), df = 47)` gives the central interval $[29.956,67.821]$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Replacing $\sigma^2$ with the same sample variance makes $(n-1)S^2/S^2=n-1$ identically, erasing the comparison to an unknown population variance. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Joint normal sampling makes orthogonal linear projections independent; that
   conclusion does not hold for an arbitrary nonnormal sample.

</details>

A chi-squared variable is a sum of independent squared standard normals. When
a sample is centered, one mean direction is projected out; the resulting
variance statistic has $n-1$ degrees of freedom only under independent normal
sampling. The [Student-$t$ distribution](student-t-distribution.qmd) next
combines this variance component with a standardized sample mean.
